reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and benign breast disease guidance
clinicalPearls: An intraductal papilloma is a benign wart-like growth within a breast duct and is the commonest cause of pathological bloodstained or serous single-duct nipple discharge
A solitary (central) papilloma typically arises in a large subareolar duct in middle-aged women and presents with spontaneous discharge from a single duct
Multiple (peripheral) papillomas occur in younger women, are located more peripherally, and carry a somewhat higher associated risk of malignancy
A small subareolar lump may be palpable, and gentle pressure at a specific point around the areola may reproduce discharge from the responsible duct
Triple assessment is used to evaluate the discharge and any mass and to exclude an underlying carcinoma
Ultrasound may show a dilated duct containing a mass, and ductography or ductoscopy can localise the lesion in selected cases
Definitive management is usually excision of the affected duct (microdochectomy) or a total duct excision, which provides both treatment and full histology
Because a papilloma can harbour or be associated with atypia or malignancy, thorough histological assessment of the excised lesion is important
reference.pathophysiology: An intraductal papilloma is a benign proliferation of ductal epithelium supported by fibrovascular cores that projects into the lumen of a breast duct. Its delicate, highly vascular fronds are fragile and bleed easily, which accounts for the characteristic bloodstained or serous nipple discharge, and the growth may partially obstruct the duct producing localised dilatation. Solitary central lesions are generally isolated benign growths, whereas multiple peripheral papillomas represent a more diffuse proliferative process associated with a modestly increased risk of concurrent or subsequent malignancy, so histological confirmation is important to detect any atypia.
additionalDifferentials: Ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination characterising the discharge and identifying a trigger point or lump
Assessment of the discharge, including testing for blood
Ultrasound of the subareolar ducts as part of triple assessment
Mammography in women of appropriate age
Ductography or ductoscopy to localise the lesion in selected cases
Duct excision (microdochectomy) with histology for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: Bloodstained single-duct discharge, which mandates exclusion of malignancy
An associated hard or irregular mass or suspicious imaging
Atypia or malignancy identified on biopsy or excision histology
Multiple peripheral papillomas, given the higher associated cancer risk
reference.prognosis: A solitary intraductal papilloma is benign and generally cured by duct excision with an excellent prognosis, whereas multiple peripheral papillomas or lesions with atypia warrant closer surveillance because of their higher associated risk of malignancy.
pitfalls: Attributing bloodstained single-duct discharge to a benign papilloma without excluding carcinoma
Relying on imaging alone and not obtaining histology of the affected duct
Underestimating the malignancy risk associated with multiple peripheral papillomas
Failing to identify the responsible duct before surgery, leading to incomplete excision
Confusing pathological single-duct discharge with benign physiological discharge
